claim: Salmonella Typhi is the causative agent of typhoid.
source: Salmonella Typhi is the causative agent of typhoid.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the etiology of typhoid fever.

claim: Typhoid is diagnosed by blood culture, a method that lacks sensitivity, portability and speed.
source: Typhoid is diagnosed by blood culture, a method that lacks sensitivity, portability and speed.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about blood culture limitations in typhoid diagnosis.

claim: Specific metabolomic profiles can be detected in the blood of typhoid patients from Nepal.
source: We have previously shown that specific metabolomic profiles can be detected in the blood of typhoid patients from Nepal (Näsström et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Mass spectrometry was performed on plasma from Bangladeshi and Senegalese patients with culture confirmed typhoid fever, clinically suspected typhoid, and other febrile diseases including malaria.
source: Here, we performed mass spectrometry on plasma from Bangladeshi and Senegalese patients with culture confirmed typhoid fever, clinically suspected typhoid, and other febrile diseases including malaria.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology performed in the current study.

claim: Supervised pattern recognition modelling can significantly distinguish metabolite profiles in plasma from culture confirmed typhoid patients.
source: After applying supervised pattern recognition modelling, we could significantly distinguish metabolite profiles in plasma from the culture confirmed typhoid patients.
evidence: This is based on the data analysis results from the study.

claim: 24 metabolites were consistently up- or down regulated in the Bangladeshi/Senegalese validation cohort and the Nepali cohort.
source: After comparing the direction of change and degree of multivariate significance, we identified 24 metabolites that were consistently up- or down regulated in a further Bangladeshi/Senegalese validation cohort, and the Nepali cohort from our previous work.
evidence: This is a direct result from the comparative analysis of metabolite data across cohorts.

claim: A metabolite panel can distinguish typhoid from other febrile diseases.
source: We have identified and validated a metabolite panel that can distinguish typhoid from other febrile diseases, providing a new approach for typhoid diagnostics.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data and validation.

claim: There are an estimated 21 million typhoid cases annually.
source: With an estimated 21 million cases annually, typhoid remains a persistent global health issue (Buckle et al., 2012; Ochiai et al., 2008).
evidence: This epidemiological estimate is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Typhoid remains a persistent global health issue.
source: With an estimated 21 million cases annually, typhoid remains a persistent global health issue (Buckle et al., 2012; Ochiai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited case burden and references to published literature.

claim: The symptoms of typhoid arise after the organism invades the gastrointestinal wall and enters the bloodstream.
source: The symptoms of typhoid arise after the organism invades the gastrointestinal wall and enters the bloodstream (Everest et al., 2001).
evidence: This pathophysiological mechanism is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Isolating the organism from the bloodstream is the mainstay of typhoid diagnostics.
source: Isolating the organism from the bloodstream is the mainstay of typhoid diagnostics (Gilman et al., 1975; Parry et al., 2011)
evidence: This diagnostic standard is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Blood culture for typhoid diagnosis lacks sensitivity.
source: Isolating the organism from the bloodstream is the mainstay of typhoid diagnostics (Gilman et al., 1975; Parry et al., 2011), but this method lacks sensitivity
evidence: This limitation is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Researchers are aiming to discover biomarkers that may become a more reliable and rapid approach to diagnosing typhoid disease.
source: but this method lacks sensitivity and researchers are aiming to discover biomarkers that may become a more reliable and rapid approach to diagnosing disease (Baker et al., 2010).
evidence: This research direction is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Metabolomics is a method detecting low-molecular-weight metabolites in biological materials by mass spectrometry.
source: One approach for discovering biomarkers is metabolomics, a method detecting low-molecular-weight metabolites in biological materials by mass spectrometry (Madsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This definition of metabolomics is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Significant and reproducible metabolite profiles could segregate S. Typhi cases, Salmonella Paratyphi A cases, and asymptomatic controls in a Nepali patient cohort.
source: Our previous work demonstrated that significant and reproducible metabolite profiles could segregate S. Typhi cases, Salmonella Paratyphi A cases, and asymptomatic controls in a Nepali patient cohort (Näsström et al., 2014).
evidence: This finding from previous work is supported by citation to the authors' prior publication.

claim: A combination of six metabolites could define the infecting pathogen in the blood of febrile patients.
source: Further, we found that a combination of six metabolites could define the infecting pathogen in the blood of febrile patients.
evidence: This refers to findings from the authors' previous work.

claim: 394 peaks were resolved from the GCxGC-TOFMS data by hierarchical multivariate curve resolution in 30 plasma samples from febrile patients in Bangladesh.
source: By hierarchical multivariate curve resolution, we resolved 394 peaks from the GCxGC-TOFMS data (Materials and methods) in 30 plasma samples from febrile patients in Bangladesh (Table 1)
evidence: This is a direct result from the data processing methodology applied to the samples.

claim: 236 metabolite peaks were suitable for modeling after filtering to remove low-quality peaks and metabolites with a high run order correlation.
source: after filtering to remove low-quality peaks and metabolites with a high run order correlation we detected 236 metabolite peaks suitable for modeling.
evidence: This describes the data processing and quality control steps applied.

claim: 65/236 (27.5%) of detected metabolite peaks had a putative annotation.
source: Of the detected metabolite peaks, 65/236 (27.5%) had a putative annotation
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the metabolite identification process.

claim: 8/236 (3.4%) of detected metabolite peaks had a metabolite class.
source: 8/236 (3.4%) had a metabolite class
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the metabolite classification process.

claim: 32/236 (13.6%) of detected metabolite peaks were of uncertain identity.
source: 32/236 (13.6%) were of uncertain identity
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the metabolite identification process.

claim: 131/236 (55.5%) of detected metabolite peaks were unknown.
source: 131/236 (55.5%) were unknown
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the metabolite identification process.

claim: One outlying sample in the fever control group was excluded from initial modeling.
source: Initial modeling of these 236 metabolites revealed one outlying sample in the fever control group, which was excluded.
evidence: This describes a data quality control decision made during analysis.

claim: The OPLS-DA model provided excellent predictive power for distinguishing between culture-positive typhoid patients and fever controls using 236 informative primary metabolite features (p=0.006).
source: The OPLS-DA model provided excellent predictive power for distinguishing between culture-positive typhoid patients and fever controls in the first predictive component using 236 informative primary metabolite features (t[1] and tcv[1]) (p=0.006) (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the supervised pattern recognition modeling with reference to figure showing the separation.

claim: A major challenge in diagnosing typhoid is identifying true typhoid patients who have a negative blood culture result.
source: A major challenge in diagnosing typhoid is identifying true typhoid patients but have a negative blood culture result (Moore et al., 2014).
evidence: This diagnostic challenge is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: There was significant overlap between the culture-negative/clinically suspected typhoid metabolite profiles with both the culture-positive group and the fever control group.
source: We observed a significant overlap between the culture-negative/clinically suspected typhoid metabolite profiles with both the culture-positive group and the fever control group (Figure 1B).
evidence: This observation is based on the data analysis results shown in the figure.

claim: 5/9 plasma samples from clinically suspected typhoid had a metabolite profile indicative of culture-positive typhoid.
source: We found that 5/9 plasma samples had a metabolite profile indicative of culture-positive typhoid and three exhibited a greater degree of resemblance to fever controls (one indifferent) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the predictive modeling analysis.

claim: 3/5 clinically suspected typhoid samples with a metabolite profile indicative of typhoid were additionally PCR amplification positive for S. Typhi in blood.
source: Notably, 3/5 clinically suspected typhoid samples with a metabolite profile indicative of typhoid were additionally PCR amplification positive for S. Typhi in blood (Table 1 and Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a result from comparing metabolite predictions with PCR test results.

claim: 941 putative metabolite peaks were obtained from urine using positive ionization UPLC-Q-TOFMS.
source: Examination of 941 putative metabolite peaks obtained from urine using positive ionization an OPLS-DA model resulted in significantly different metabolite profiles between the S. Typhiculture-positive patients and the fever controls (p=0.025) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the urine sample analysis.

claim: OPLS-DA model of urine metabolites resulted in significantly different metabolite profiles between S. Typhi culture-positive patients and fever controls (p=0.025).
source: Examination of 941 putative metabolite peaks obtained from urine using positive ionization an OPLS-DA model resulted in significantly different metabolite profiles between the S. Typhiculture-positive patients and the fever controls (p=0.025) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the supervised pattern recognition modeling of urine samples.

claim: 99 informative metabolites in plasma were found in both Bangladeshi and Nepali cohorts.
source: We found 99 informative metabolites in plasma from both cohorts.
evidence: This is a result from comparing metabolite data between the two cohorts.

claim: 33 metabolites were consistently up- or downregulated between culture-positive S. Typhi patients and fever/asymptomatic controls in the Bangladeshi and Nepali studies.
source: Comparing the direction of change and the degree of significance we identified 33 metabolites that were consistently up- or downregulated between the culture-positive S. Typhi patients and fever/asymptomatic controls in the two studies (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative analysis of metabolite patterns across cohorts.

claim: 15 of the 33 metabolites were multivariate significant with a stricter criteria (w*>|x̄ ±SD|) in the Bangladeshi cohort.
source: Fifteen of the 33 metabolites were multivariate significant with a stricter criteria (w*>|x¯ ±SD|) in the Bangladeshi cohort
evidence: This is a statistical result from applying significance criteria to the metabolite data.

claim: All 33 metabolites were multivariate significant (w*>|0.03|) in the Nepali cohort.
source: all 33 metabolites were multivariate significant (w*>|0.03|) in the Nepali cohort.
evidence: This is a statistical result from applying significance criteria to the metabolite data.

claim: OPLS-DA models with the 15 multivariate significant metabolites resulted in significant separations between S. Typhi culture-positive patients and fever controls in the Bangladeshi cohort (p=0.016).
source: OPLS-DA models with the 15 multivariate significant metabolites resulted in significant separations between S. Typhiculture-positive patients and fever controls in the current study (Bangladeshi cohort) (p=0.016), and the asymptomatic controls in the previous study (Nepali cohort) (p<0.0001) (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the supervised pattern recognition modeling.

claim: OPLS-DA models with the 15 multivariate significant metabolites resulted in significant separations between S. Typhi culture-positive patients and asymptomatic controls in the Nepali cohort (p<0.0001).
source: OPLS-DA models with the 15 multivariate significant metabolites resulted in significant separations between S. Typhiculture-positive patients and fever controls in the current study (Bangladeshi cohort) (p=0.016), and the asymptomatic controls in the previous study (Nepali cohort) (p<0.0001) (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the supervised pattern recognition modeling.

claim: Models based on all 33 correspondingly up or downregulated metabolites could distinguish S. Typhi culture-positive patients from fever/asymptomatic controls in the current study (p=0.077).
source: Models based on all 33 correspondingly up or downregulated metabolites could also distinguish the S. Typhiculture-positive patients from the fever/asymptomatic controls (current study: p=0.077, previous study: p<0.0001) (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the supervised pattern recognition modeling.

claim: Models based on all 33 correspondingly up or downregulated metabolites could distinguish S. Typhi culture-positive patients from fever/asymptomatic controls in the previous study (p<0.0001).
source: Models based on all 33 correspondingly up or downregulated metabolites could also distinguish the S. Typhiculture-positive patients from the fever/asymptomatic controls (current study: p=0.077, previous study: p<0.0001) (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the supervised pattern recognition modeling.

claim: 54 plasma samples from febrile patients from Bangladesh and Senegal were analyzed using GC-TOFMS for validation.
source: For further validation, we analyzed an additional 54 plasma samples from febrile patients from Bangladesh and Senegal using a different analytical technique (GC-TOFMS, methods).
evidence: This describes the validation cohort and analytical method used.

claim: The validation cohort included samples from patients with confirmed typhoid and samples from patients with malaria or infections caused by other pathogens.
source: This validation cohort included samples from patients with confirmed typhoid and samples from patients with malaria or infections caused by other pathogens.
evidence: This describes the composition of the validation cohort.

claim: 247 putative metabolites were detected through an independent targeted processing approach in the validation cohort.
source: Through an independent targeted processing approach, we detected 247 putative metabolites
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data processing of the validation cohort.

claim: 104 metabolites were suitable for modeling after manual filtering in the validation cohort.
source: after manual filtering, 104 metabolites were suitable for modeling (Supplementary file 1D).

claim: A three-class OPLS-DA model indicated the discrimination of typhoid samples from the two control groups (malaria and other pathogens).
source: Initially, a three-class OPLS-DA model was obtained indicating the discrimination of typhoid samples from the two control groups (malaria and other pathogens) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a result from the multivariate modeling analysis.

claim: A two-class OPLS-DA model for separation between typhoid and all control samples together showed significant separation for the new Bangladeshi samples (one overlapping control) and the majority of the Senegalese samples (p<0.0001).
source: Furthermore, a two-class OPLS-DA model for separation between typhoid and all control samples together showed significant separation for the new Bangladeshi samples (one overlapping control) and the majority of the Senegalese samples (p<0.0001) (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the supervised pattern recognition modeling.

claim: Malaria presents with a clinical syndrome that can be indistinguishable from typhoid fever.
source: Malaria presents with a clinical syndrome that can be indistinguishable from typhoid fever
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about the overlapping presentations of these diseases.

claim: Typhoid samples were significantly separated from malaria positive samples in an OPLS-DA model (p=0.0001), with two overlapping Senegalese typhoid samples.
source: The typhoid samples were compared to the malaria positive samples in a separate OPLS-DA model and showed significant separation (p=0.0001), with two overlapping Senegalese typhoid samples, potentially signifying co-infection (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the supervised pattern recognition modeling.

claim: Two overlapping Senegalese typhoid samples in the malaria comparison potentially signify co-infection.
source: with two overlapping Senegalese typhoid samples, potentially signifying co-infection
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed overlap in metabolite profiles.

claim: 49 common metabolites were identified across all datasets (Bangladeshi/Senegalese validation cohort, primary Bangladeshi cohort, and Nepali cohort).
source: We identified 49 common metabolites across all datasets.
evidence: This is a result from comparing metabolite data across all three cohorts.

claim: 24 metabolites were consistently up- or downregulated in the Bangladeshi/Senegalese validation cohort and the Bangladeshi cohort and/or the Nepali cohort.
source: After comparing the direction of change and degree of multivariate significance, we found 24 metabolites that were consistently up- or downregulated in the Bangladeshi/Senegalese validation cohort and the Bangladeshi cohort and/or the Nepali cohort (Supplementary file 1D).

claim: OPLS-DA models of the consistently up- or downregulated metabolites resulted in significant separations between those with typhoid and control samples for the Bangladeshi/Senegalese validation cohort (p<0.0001).
source: OPLS-DA models of the consistently up- or downregulated metabolites resulted in significant separations between those with typhoid and the control samples for the Bangladeshi/Senegalese validation cohort (p<0.0001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A)

claim: OPLS-DA models of the consistently up- or downregulated metabolites resulted in significant separations between those with typhoid and control samples for the Nepali cohort (p<0.0001).
